title: API pagination and filtering
subtitle: Offset and cursor pagination, stable sort orders, filters and page sizes, and why deep offsets get slow on big tables.

c.v: A shop has an admin page for orders. It calls
. In the first year, the table holds 20,000 orders, and every page loads fast.

Two years later, the table holds 30 million orders. A finance tool walks through all orders every night, page by page. The first pages take a few milliseconds. Page 100,000 takes seconds, and the whole job never ends before morning.

The support team reports a second problem. During a sale, they scroll the list of new orders. Some orders appear twice, and some never appear at all. New orders arrive every second and push the rest down.
The team moves to a cursor that remembers the last order seen. Every page is now fast, and nothing repeats. This story is made up. Slack, however, left offsets for the same two reasons.
You never return a whole list in one answer. You return it in pages. The

Most APIs hide the "last one I saw" inside a token called a cursor.
An offset remembers a position, and positions move when data changes. A cursor remembers a row, and a row stays where it is.
Step through two pages of a list, with a new row between them. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Offset, and why deep pages get slow.
skips 40 rows and returns the next 20. PostgreSQL's docs say the skipped rows "still have to be computed inside the server", so a large offset can be slow.
Markus Winand shows the same thing. The database must count all rows from the start until it reaches the page, so later pages take longer.
Page 1 is cheap. Page 100,000 reads millions of rows to throw them away.

Offsets also drift. When a row is inserted above the reader's position, the next page starts one row too early and repeats a row. When a row is deleted, the next page starts one row too late and skips one. Slack's example: you read 10 messages, 10 new ones arrive, and page two shows the same messages again.

Clients never read the cursor, so they would not see that change. Google's AIP-158 says page tokens must be opaque and must not be user-parseable. Plain Base64 is not enough to hide what is inside, so Google says to do more than that. It also says a token only marks where to continue. It never grants access, so check permissions on every request.
Cursors can expire. Slack tells clients not to keep cursors for hours or days.
Google says tokens may expire after a reasonable time and suggests about three days.
Filters and sort order are query parameters, for example

. Our advice: only allow sorts that have an index. Without one, each page may need to sort the whole table. Google says the other parameters must stay the same while a client follows page tokens, and the API should return an error if they change. Only the page size may change.
Put the filter and sort inside the cursor too, so the server can check them.

q.v: Your list endpoint uses ORDER BY created_at with OFFSET and LIMIT. Many rows share the same created_at. What can go wrong?

options.v: Nothing. The database keeps the same order every time.
Rows with the same time can come back in a different order, so pages can repeat or skip them. Add a unique column like id to the sort.
The query will fail with an error.

why.v: PostgreSQL says LIMIT needs an ORDER BY that gives a unique order, or you get an unpredictable subset of rows.

q.v: Why does ?offset=500000&limit=20 get slow on a big table?

options.v: The database still has to produce the 500,000 skipped rows before it returns 20.

why.v: PostgreSQL's docs say rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server.

q.v: Why should a cursor be opaque, instead of a plain id the client builds?

options.v: You can change what is inside it later without breaking clients, because they never read it.

why.v: Google AIP-158 says tokens must not be user-parseable, and the Relay spec says clients should treat cursors as opaque. Slack shows how one cursor could hold a position for each shard.

q.v: In the Relay spec, which fields must a connection type have?

why.v: The spec says connection types must have fields named edges and pageInfo. data and has_more are Stripe's names.
